primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: X-linked Alport syndrome due to COL4A5 pathogenic variant
mechanism: COL4A5 encodes the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen, a component of basement-membrane collagen networks; pathogenic variants disrupt the alpha3-alpha4-alpha5 type IV collagen network in the glomerular basement membrane and can also affect cochlear and ocular basement membranes.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. His maternal uncle developed kidney failure at a young age. Molecular testing identifies a pathogenic variant in COL4A5.
lead: Which protein is directly encoded by the mutated gene in this patient?
correct: The alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen
distractors: The alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
The alpha-4 chain of type IV collagen
The alpha-1 chain of type I collagen
Fibrillin-1
distractor_notes: COL4A3 encodes the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen and can cause autosomal Alport syndromes, but it is not the gene identified in this stem.
COL4A4 encodes the alpha-4 chain of type IV collagen and can cause autosomal Alport syndromes, but it is not the gene identified in this stem.
Type I collagen alpha chains are encoded by COL1A genes and are associated with disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta, not COL4A5-related Alport syndrome.
Fibrillin-1 is encoded by FBN1 and is associated with Marfan syndrome, not Alport syndrome.
key_expl: COL4A5 encodes collagen alpha-5(IV). X-linked Alport syndrome commonly results from pathogenic COL4A5 variants and affects the glomerular basement membrane, with characteristic renal, auditory, and ocular manifestations.
objective: Link COL4A5-related X-linked Alport syndrome to the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Activated factor XIII is a transglutaminase that covalently cross-links fibrin after fibrin formation, stabilizing the clot; factor XIII deficiency can cause significant delayed bleeding despite normal PT and aPTT because routine clotting times measure events before factor XIII-mediated cross-linking.
vignette: A child has recurrent delayed bleeding after minor trauma and a history of prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump. Platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time are normal.
lead: Which hemostatic step is most directly impaired in this disorder?
correct: Covalent cross-linking of fibrin strands after fibrin formation
distractors: Thrombin-mediated cleavage of fibrinogen to fibrin
Activation of factor X by the intrinsic tenase complex
Von Willebrand factor-mediated platelet adhesion to subendothelium
Gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors
distractor_notes: Defective thrombin generation or fibrinogen cleavage would generally disturb earlier coagulation steps and can alter routine clotting tests; factor XIII acts after fibrin is formed.
Intrinsic-tenase defects such as factor VIII or IX deficiency typically prolong the aPTT.
Von Willebrand factor defects primarily impair platelet adhesion and may alter factor VIII levels; they do not explain the classic normal-PT/aPTT factor XIII pattern.
Defective gamma-carboxylation affects vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X and typically alters PT and/or aPTT rather than isolated post-fibrin clot stabilization.
key_expl: Factor XIII is the fibrin-stabilizing transglutaminase. It cross-links fibrin after the clot has formed, so severe deficiency can produce delayed bleeding while PT and aPTT remain normal.
objective: Recognize factor XIII deficiency as a defect of post-formation fibrin cross-linking that is not detected by routine PT/aPTT testing.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Miller Fisher syndrome associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies
mechanism: Miller Fisher syndrome is an acute immune-mediated Guillain-Barre-spectrum neuropathy classically characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia and is strongly associated with IgG antibodies against the GQ1b ganglioside.
vignette: A 34-year-old man develops diplopia, gait unsteadiness, and absent deep-tendon reflexes 10 days after a diarrheal illness. Strength in the limbs is preserved, and mental status is normal.
lead: Which autoantibody is most strongly associated with this syndrome?
distractors: IgG antibody against GM1 ganglioside
Antibody against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels
Antibody against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Antibody against aquaporin-4 water channels
distractor_notes: Anti-GM1 antibodies are more strongly associated with axonal Guillain-Barre variants such as acute motor axonal neuropathy rather than the classic Miller Fisher triad.
P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine-receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis.
Aquaporin-4 antibodies are associated with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
key_expl: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia after an infection is characteristic of Miller Fisher syndrome. Anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies are found in most affected patients and are strongly associated with this phenotype.
objective: Recognize Miller Fisher syndrome and associate it with anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva due to ACVR1 gain of function
mechanism: Gain-of-function pathogenic variants in ACVR1/ALK2 cause dysregulated bone morphogenetic protein signaling and progressive heterotopic endochondral ossification of skeletal muscle, fascia, tendons, and ligaments, often triggered by soft-tissue injury.
vignette: A child is born with malformed great toes and later develops recurrent painful soft-tissue swellings that progressively ossify after minor trauma. A biopsy of a new lesion is being considered.
lead: Which molecular abnormality most likely underlies this disorder?
correct: Gain-of-function signaling through the ACVR1 bone morphogenetic protein receptor
distractors: Loss of RYR1-mediated calcium release from skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum
Loss of dystrophin linking the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix
Loss of type I collagen synthesis from COL1A1
Gain-of-function signaling through FGFR3 in growth-plate chondrocytes
distractor_notes: RYR1 abnormalities cause malignant hyperthermia susceptibility or congenital myopathies, not progressive heterotopic ossification with malformed great toes.
Dystrophin deficiency causes Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy.
COL1A1 defects cause disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta rather than heterotopic endochondral bone formation.
FGFR3 gain of function causes achondroplasia and suppresses growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation; it does not cause fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva.
key_expl: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is caused by activating ACVR1/ALK2 variants that dysregulate BMP signaling and cause progressive heterotopic endochondral ossification. Trauma can precipitate new lesions, so biopsy can worsen disease.
objective: Link fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva to ACVR1 gain-of-function signaling and trauma-triggered heterotopic ossification.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Transthyretin amyloidosis results from destabilization of transthyretin tetramers and extracellular deposition of misfolded transthyretin fibrils; myocardial infiltration increases ventricular wall thickness and stiffness and produces a restrictive cardiomyopathy.
vignette: A 76-year-old man has progressive exertional dyspnea, edema, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. He previously underwent surgery for bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. Echocardiography shows increased ventricular wall thickness, but the ECG has relatively low QRS voltage. Serum and urine immunofixation and the serum free-light-chain ratio show no evidence of a monoclonal protein. Technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy shows grade 3 myocardial uptake.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's cardiac disease?
distractors: Immunoglobulin light-chain cardiac amyloidosis
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to a sarcomeric mutation
Hypertensive left ventricular hypertrophy
Cardiac hemochromatosis
distractor_notes: AL cardiac amyloidosis can cause a similar infiltrative cardiomyopathy, but the absence of monoclonal protein together with strong grade 2/3 bone-tracer uptake specifically supports ATTR cardiac amyloidosis.
Sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can increase wall thickness but does not explain the amyloid scintigraphy pattern and extracardiac carpal-tunnel clue.

Chronic hypertension can cause left-ventricular hypertrophy but does not produce grade 3 technetium-pyrophosphate myocardial uptake characteristic of ATTR in the appropriate monoclonal-protein-negative setting.
Cardiac iron overload typically produces a different infiltrative process evaluated with iron studies and cardiac MRI and does not explain the ATTR scintigraphy pattern.
key_expl: In a patient with imaging features of cardiac amyloidosis, grade 2 or 3 technetium-pyrophosphate myocardial uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein can establish ATTR cardiac amyloidosis noninvasively. Older age and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome are additional ATTR clues.
objective: Recognize transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis from restrictive cardiac findings plus strong bone-tracer uptake after exclusion of a monoclonal light-chain process.
clues: increased wall thickness with relatively low ECG voltage

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary fructose intolerance due to aldolase B deficiency
mechanism: Aldolase B deficiency prevents cleavage of fructose-1-phosphate into glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone phosphate; fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, traps phosphate, depletes ATP, and inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
vignette: An 8-month-old infant develops vomiting, lethargy, hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly after fruit puree and juice are introduced. The infant becomes well when these foods are avoided and later strongly avoids sweet foods.
lead: Which metabolite accumulates directly because of the deficient enzyme in this disorder?
distractors: Fructose-6-phosphate
Galactose-1-phosphate
Sorbitol
Glucose-1-phosphate
distractor_notes: Fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate and is not the substrate that accumulates when aldolase B is deficient.
Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in classic galactosemia due to GALT deficiency.
Sorbitol can accumulate in tissues during hyperglycemia through the polyol pathway but is not the defining metabolite of hereditary fructose intolerance.
Glucose-1-phosphate is generated during glycogenolysis and is not the direct substrate of aldolase B.
key_expl: Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate. In hereditary fructose intolerance, fructose-1-phosphate accumulates after fructose exposure and contributes to phosphate depletion, ATP depletion, and inhibition of hepatic glucose production.
objective: Identify fructose-1-phosphate accumulation as the direct metabolic consequence of aldolase B deficiency in hereditary fructose intolerance.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: TPO-related congenital hypothyroidism due to thyroid dyshormonogenesis
mechanism: Thyroid peroxidase at the apical follicular-cell membrane uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidize iodide and catalyzes iodination (organification) of tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin, a required step in thyroid-hormone synthesis; loss-of-function TPO variants impair this process.
vignette: A newborn screen shows low thyroxine and markedly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone. Examination reveals a goiter, and imaging confirms a normally located thyroid gland. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in TPO.
lead: Which biochemical reaction is most directly impaired by this enzyme deficiency?
correct: Oxidation of iodide and incorporation of iodine into tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin
distractors: Basolateral uptake of iodide into thyroid follicular cells through the sodium-iodide symporter
Synthesis and secretion of thyroglobulin by thyroid follicular cells
Proteolytic release of T3 and T4 from iodinated thyroglobulin in lysosomes
Binding of thyroid-stimulating hormone to its Gs-coupled receptor
distractor_notes: Basolateral iodide uptake is mediated by the sodium-iodide symporter, not thyroid peroxidase.
Thyroglobulin synthesis is encoded by TG and is distinct from the TPO-catalyzed organification reaction.
Proteolysis of iodinated thyroglobulin releases thyroid hormones after organification and coupling have already occurred; it is not the direct TPO-catalyzed step.
TSH-receptor binding and Gs-cAMP signaling regulate thyroid function but are not the enzymatic reaction performed by TPO.
key_expl: Thyroid peroxidase catalyzes iodide oxidation and organification of iodine onto thyroglobulin tyrosyl residues at the apical follicular-cell surface. TPO loss therefore causes thyroid dyshormonogenesis with congenital hypothyroidism, often with goiter.
objective: Link TPO-related congenital hypothyroidism to failure of iodide oxidation and organification onto thyroglobulin.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Adult Refsum disease due to impaired phytanic-acid alpha-oxidation
mechanism: Most adult Refsum disease is caused by biallelic PHYH variants that impair peroxisomal phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, blocking alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid and causing systemic phytanic-acid accumulation.
vignette: A 24-year-old man has progressive retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, and ichthyosis. Plasma phytanic acid is markedly elevated, whereas very-long-chain fatty acid concentrations are normal.
lead: Which metabolic process is most directly impaired?
distractors: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids
Mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids
Lysosomal degradation of galactocerebroside
Mitochondrial oxidation of branched-chain amino acids
distractor_notes: Impaired peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids is characteristic of disorders such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy or Zellweger-spectrum disease; VLCFAs are normal in adult Refsum disease.
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes fasting-related hypoketotic hypoglycemia, not phytanic-acid accumulation with retinitis pigmentosa and ichthyosis.
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease.
Branched-chain amino-acid oxidation is impaired in maple syrup urine disease and does not explain phytanic-acid accumulation.
key_expl: Adult Refsum disease is a peroxisomal alpha-oxidation disorder. PHYH deficiency prevents normal phytanic-acid degradation, leading to accumulation and the characteristic retinal, neurologic, auditory, skin, and cardiac manifestations.
objective: Associate adult Refsum disease with impaired peroxisomal alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid due most commonly to PHYH deficiency.

diagnosis: Partial verification bias in a diagnostic-accuracy study
mechanism: Partial verification bias occurs when only a selected subset of participants who receive an index diagnostic test undergo the reference standard, often because verification is more likely after a positive index result, distorting estimates of diagnostic accuracy.
vignette: Investigators evaluate a new blood test for a disease. Every participant receives the new test, but the invasive reference-standard procedure is performed in all participants with a positive new test and in only a small nonrandom subset of those with a negative new test. Sensitivity and specificity are then estimated only among participants whose disease status was verified.
lead: Which bias most directly threatens the reported diagnostic accuracy?
distractors: Spectrum bias
Incorporation bias
Diagnostic review bias
Lead-time bias
distractor_notes: Spectrum bias arises when test performance differs because the study sample does not represent the relevant spectrum of disease and nondisease, not because reference-standard verification depends on the index result.
Incorporation bias occurs when the index test itself is included in the reference standard used to define disease status.
Diagnostic review bias occurs when interpretation of the reference standard is influenced by knowledge of the index-test result; the central defect here is selective verification.
Lead-time bias is a screening-survival artifact and is unrelated to selective application of a diagnostic reference standard.
key_expl: Only a selected subset receives the reference standard, with verification strongly influenced by the index-test result. This is partial verification, or work-up, bias and can distort sensitivity and specificity estimates.
objective: Identify partial verification bias when reference-standard confirmation is selectively performed after an index diagnostic test.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Menkes disease due to ATP7A loss of function
mechanism: ATP7A is a copper-transporting ATPase that supports intracellular copper delivery and copper efflux from enterocytes; loss of ATP7A traps copper in intestinal cells and produces systemic copper deficiency with impaired copper-dependent enzymes.
vignette: A 3-month-old boy has failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, and sparse, brittle, kinky hair. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin concentrations are low.
lead: Which transport defect most directly causes the systemic copper deficiency in this disorder?
correct: Impaired ATP7A-mediated copper efflux from intestinal enterocytes
distractors: Impaired ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion from hepatocytes
Impaired ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes
Impaired intestinal uptake of heme iron through heme transport pathways
Excess intestinal copper absorption with defective hepatic storage
distractor_notes: ATP7B loss causes Wilson disease by reducing biliary copper excretion and promoting copper accumulation rather than systemic copper deficiency from intestinal trapping.
Ferroportin exports iron, not copper, from enterocytes.
Heme-iron uptake pathways do not explain the characteristic copper deficiency, kinky hair, and ATP7A phenotype.
Menkes disease reflects impaired copper transport/efflux rather than excessive intestinal copper absorption.
key_expl: ATP7A loss prevents normal copper trafficking and efflux from enterocytes, causing intestinal copper trapping and systemic copper deficiency. Reduced activity of copper-dependent enzymes contributes to the neurologic, connective-tissue, and hair abnormalities.
objective: Explain Menkes disease as ATP7A-dependent failure of intestinal copper efflux and systemic copper delivery.
